notes.front: What is a Product Backlog item (PBI)?
notes.back: An item in the Product Backlog, the emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product.
notes.explanation: Items are what the Product Owner creates, communicates and orders, and what refinement breaks down.
notes.evidence: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product.
notes.example: “Let patients reschedule an appointment online” as one entry near the top of a clinic booking system’s Product Backlog.

notes.front: What is a Nexus?
notes.back: A group of Scrum Teams that work together to deliver a single product.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide adds that it is “a connection between people and things”, and it extends Scrum only where multiple teams need it.
notes.evidence: A Nexus is a group of approximately three to nine Scrum Teams that work together to deliver a single product; it is a connection between people and things.
notes.example: Like one Scrum Team, but scaled out: five teams building one ticketing app together.

notes.front: In Nexus, what is the Integrated Increment?
notes.back: The current sum of all integrated work completed by a Nexus toward the Product Goal.
notes.explanation: It must meet the Definition of Done, and it is inspected at the Nexus Sprint Review.
notes.evidence: The Integrated Increment represents the current sum of all integrated work completed by a Nexus toward the Product Goal.
notes.example: Like a single team’s Increment, but holding every team’s pieces joined together: the catalogue and the checkout working as one build.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Integration Team accountable for?
notes.back: Ensuring that a done Integrated Increment (the combined work of the Nexus) is produced at least once a Sprint.
notes.explanation: Nexus introduces it as an additional accountability on top of the three the Scrum Guide defines.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is accountable for ensuring that a done Integrated Increment (the combined work completed by a Nexus) is produced at least once a Sprint.
notes.example: Like a Scrum Team’s aim of a done Increment each Sprint, but held for the combined output of all the teams.

notes.front: In Nexus, what is Cross-Team Refinement?
notes.back: Refinement of the Product Backlog across the Nexus that reduces or eliminates cross-team dependencies.
notes.explanation: The Product Backlog must be broken down so that dependencies become transparent and are removed or minimized.
notes.evidence: Cross-Team Refinement of the Product Backlog reduces or eliminates cross-team dependencies within a Nexus.
notes.example: Like one team’s refinement, but with several teams at the table so that work touching more than one team shows up early.

notes.front: What is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team?
notes.back: The Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes it as an emergent, ordered list, so whatever the team works on appears there.
notes.evidence: It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.

notes.front: Is the Product Backlog fixed at the start, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: No. It is emergent: an ordered list of what is needed to improve the product.
notes.explanation: Emergent means it keeps growing and changing; it may even be adjusted at the Sprint Review to meet new opportunities.
notes.evidence: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product.

notes.front: A team keeps its technical tasks on a separate list outside the Product Backlog and works from both lists. How does this compare with the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: B) The Product Backlog is meant to be the single source of work, so the tasks belong in it.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls the Product Backlog the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team, and its ordering is the Product Owner’s.
notes.choices:
A) It is fine, as long as the Developers own the second list
B) The Product Backlog is meant to be the single source of work, so the tasks belong in it
C) It is fine if the Scrum Master approves the second list
notes.choicesExplained: A and C keep two sources of work; the Guide names one single source.
notes.evidence: It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.

notes.front: Which word does the Scrum Guide use for arranging the Product Backlog: “prioritizing” or “ordering”?
notes.back: “Ordering”: ordering Product Backlog items is part of the Product Owner’s accountability.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls the Product Backlog an “ordered” list and lists “Ordering Product Backlog items” among the Product Owner’s duties.
notes.evidence: Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items; - Ordering Product Backlog items; and,

notes.front: Two stakeholders disagree about which of their items should come first in the Product Backlog. Who decides the order?
notes.back: A) The Product Owner.
notes.explanation: Ordering is part of the Product Owner’s accountability, and stakeholders influence it by convincing the Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) The Product Owner
B) The Developers, by vote
C) The more senior stakeholder
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Developers size items but do not order them. C: seniority does not change who is accountable for ordering.
notes.evidence: Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

notes.front: When is a Product Backlog item deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning?
notes.back: When it can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint.
notes.explanation: Readiness is about fitting inside one Sprint, which is what refining activities usually bring about.
notes.evidence: Product Backlog items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event.

notes.front: How do PBIs usually acquire the transparency needed to be ready for selection?
notes.back: After refining activities.
notes.explanation: The Guide says “usually”: refinement is the normal route, not a gate every item must pass the same way.
notes.evidence: They usually acquire this degree of transparency after refining activities.

notes.front: The top PBI would take the Scrum Team about three Sprints to get Done. Is it ready for selection at the next Sprint Planning?
notes.back: C) No; it should be refined into smaller items that can each be Done within one Sprint.
notes.explanation: Readiness means the item can be Done within one Sprint, and refinement breaks items into smaller, more precise ones.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the Product Owner says it is the most valuable
B) Yes, the team can carry it over three Sprints
C) No; it should be refined into smaller items that can each be Done within one Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: A: value does not make an item fit in one Sprint. B: an item that cannot be Done within one Sprint is not deemed ready.
notes.evidence: Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items.

notes.front: What is Product Backlog refinement, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: Breaking down and further defining PBIs into smaller, more precise items.
notes.explanation: It is how items usually gain the transparency they need to become ready for selection.
notes.evidence: Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items.

notes.front: Is Product Backlog refinement a one-off phase?
notes.back: No. It is an ongoing activity.
notes.explanation: Details such as description, order and size keep being added as the backlog emerges.
notes.evidence: This is an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size.

notes.front: A team holds one long refinement workshop when the product starts and never refines again. How does this compare with the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: A) Refinement is ongoing, so it should continue throughout.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes refinement as an ongoing activity, and the Product Backlog as emergent.
notes.choices:
A) Refinement is ongoing, so it should continue throughout
B) It matches the Guide: refinement happens once, up front
C) It matches if the workshop is timeboxed
notes.choicesExplained: B and C treat refinement as a single event; the Guide calls it an ongoing activity.
notes.evidence: This is an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size.

notes.front: What are two details that refinement adds to PBIs?
notes.back: Any two of: a description, order, size (among others).
notes.explanation: The Guide’s list starts with “such as”, so it is open, and attributes often vary with the domain of work.
notes.evidence: This is an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size.

notes.front: Do PBIs carry the same attributes in every kind of work?
notes.back: Not necessarily: attributes often vary with the domain of work.
notes.explanation: The Guide keeps the hedge “often”, leaving each team to choose attributes that suit its product.
notes.evidence: Attributes often vary with the domain of work.

notes.front: Who is responsible for sizing PBIs?
notes.back: The Developers who will be doing the work.
notes.explanation: The Guide assigns sizing to the people who will do the work; the Product Owner’s part is to help with trade-offs.
notes.evidence: The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing.

notes.front: How may the Product Owner influence the Developers during sizing?
notes.back: By helping them understand and select trade-offs.
notes.explanation: The Guide says “may influence”: the Product Owner shapes the choices, while the sizing stays with the Developers.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may influence the Developers by helping them understand and select trade-offs.

notes.front: The Developers size an item as large. The Product Owner writes a smaller size over it “to keep the plan on track”. What does the Scrum Guide describe instead?
notes.back: B) The Developers size the item; the Product Owner may help them understand and select trade-offs.
notes.explanation: Sizing belongs to the Developers who will do the work, and the Product Owner’s influence comes through trade-offs.
notes.choices:
A) The Product Owner has the final say on size
B) The Developers size the item; the Product Owner may help them understand and select trade-offs
C) The Scrum Master sets the size
notes.choicesExplained: A and C move sizing away from the Developers who will do the work, which is where the Guide puts it.
notes.evidence: The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing. The Product Owner may influence the Developers by helping them understand and select trade-offs.

notes.front: The Developers size a reporting item as too big for one Sprint. The Product Owner points out that exporting to one format first would still meet users’ main need. What is the Product Owner doing?
notes.back: A) Helping the Developers understand and select a trade-off.
notes.explanation: This is the influence the Guide allows the Product Owner over sizing, while the Developers still size what is left.
notes.choices:
A) Helping the Developers understand and select a trade-off
B) Sizing the item on the Developers’ behalf
C) Cancelling the item
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Product Owner has not set a size; the Developers remain responsible for it. C: the item remains, only its scope is being discussed.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may influence the Developers by helping them understand and select trade-offs.

notes.front: Where is the Product Goal, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: In the Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Product Goal is the Product Backlog’s commitment, and the rest of the backlog emerges to define what will fulfil it.
notes.evidence: The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define “what” will fulfill the Product Goal.

notes.front: What does the rest of the Product Backlog emerge to define?
notes.back: “What” will fulfil the Product Goal.
notes.explanation: The Product Goal describes a future state of the product; the other items describe the work toward it.
notes.evidence: The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define “what” will fulfill the Product Goal.

notes.front: A team’s Product Goal lives only on a strategy slide that the backlog never mentions. Where does the Scrum Guide place it?
notes.back: C) In the Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide puts the Product Goal in the Product Backlog as its commitment, so the backlog’s items can be seen to serve it.
notes.choices:
A) In the Sprint Backlog
B) In a separate strategy artifact
C) In the Product Backlog
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Sprint Backlog holds the Sprint Goal, not the Product Goal. B: the Guide defines no separate artifact for it.
notes.evidence: The Product Goal describes a future state of the product which can serve as a target for the Scrum Team to plan against. The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog.

notes.front: How many Product Goals does a Scrum Team work toward at a time?
notes.back: One: it must fulfil or abandon one objective before taking on the next.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Team is described as focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal.
notes.evidence: The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team. They must fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next.

notes.front: Leadership gives a Scrum Team two Product Goals to pursue in parallel this year. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: B) The team fulfils or abandons one Product Goal before taking on the next.
notes.explanation: The Guide sets one Product Goal at a time as the Scrum Team’s long-term objective.
notes.choices:
A) Fine, if both are in the Product Backlog
B) The team fulfils or abandons one Product Goal before taking on the next
C) Fine, if each Sprint alternates between them
notes.choicesExplained: A and C both keep two Product Goals active at once, which the Guide rules out.
notes.evidence: They must fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next.

notes.front: Scrum.org’s learning series lists Product Backlog management activities. Which one is about keeping things out of the backlog as well as putting them in?
notes.back: Deciding what the Product Backlog should contain, and what it should not.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org lists it alongside formulating a Product Goal, ordering, breaking items down and sizing them.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Backlog Management”, “Product Backlog Management Activities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Scrum.org’s list of Product Backlog management activities, which activity concerns the long-term objective?
notes.back: Formulating a Product Goal.
notes.explanation: It comes first in that series’ list of activities, before deciding what to include and ordering.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Backlog Management”, “Product Backlog Management Activities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: At the Sprint Review, what may happen to the Product Backlog?
notes.back: It may be adjusted to meet new opportunities.
notes.explanation: Attendees review what was accomplished and what has changed in their environment, then collaborate on what to do next.
notes.evidence: Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what to do next. The Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities.

notes.front: At the Sprint Review, a customer mentions that a rival has launched a feature her firm now needs. The team and Product Owner add and reorder items there and then. Is that consistent with the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: A) Yes; the Product Backlog may be adjusted at the Sprint Review to meet new opportunities.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session about what has changed and what to do next, not just a presentation.
notes.choices:
A) Yes; the Product Backlog may be adjusted at the Sprint Review to meet new opportunities
B) No; backlog changes wait for the Sprint Retrospective
C) No; the Sprint Review is only a demonstration
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Retrospective is about quality and effectiveness, not the backlog’s content. C: the Guide says the team should avoid limiting the Sprint Review to a presentation.
notes.evidence: The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.

notes.front: What happens to a Product Backlog item that does not meet the Definition of Done?
notes.back: It cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review; it returns to the Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: Only work that meets the Definition of Done becomes part of the Increment, so unfinished work goes back for future consideration.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

notes.front: An item is “90% finished” and does not yet meet the Definition of Done. The Product Owner wants to show it at the Sprint Review. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: C) It cannot be presented; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.
notes.explanation: Only items that meet the Definition of Done are part of the Increment that is inspected at the Sprint Review.
notes.choices:
A) Show it, marked as unfinished
B) Show it if stakeholders ask for it
C) It cannot be presented; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration
notes.choicesExplained: A and B both present an item that does not meet the Definition of Done, which the Guide rules out.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review.

notes.front: If several Scrum Teams work together on one product, what must they do about the Definition of Done?
notes.back: Mutually define it and comply with the same Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: Where the Definition of Done is an organizational standard, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

notes.front: Two Scrum Teams build one product. Team A’s Definition of Done includes security testing; Team B’s does not. What does the Scrum Guide require?
notes.back: B) Both teams mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires a shared Definition of Done for teams working together on one product.
notes.choices:
A) Each team keeps its own Definition of Done
B) Both teams mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done
C) The Product Owner picks the stricter one for Team B only
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps two definitions for one product. C still leaves the teams on different definitions, and the Guide asks the teams to define it together.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

notes.front: About how many Scrum Teams make up a Nexus?
notes.back: Approximately three to nine.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide gives a range, not a hard limit: it says “approximately”.
notes.evidence: A Nexus is a group of approximately three to nine Scrum Teams that work together to deliver a single product

notes.front: In a Nexus, how many Product Owners and Product Backlogs are there?
notes.back: One Product Owner, who manages one Product Backlog that all the Scrum Teams work from.
notes.explanation: Nexus scales Scrum while keeping the single Product Owner and single Product Backlog that the Scrum Guide asks for when teams share a product.
notes.evidence: A Nexus has a single Product Owner who manages a single Product Backlog from which the Scrum Teams work.

notes.front: Which member of the Nexus Integration Team is also accountable for the single Product Backlog?
notes.back: The Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide lists the Product Owner first among the Nexus Integration Team’s members.
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team consists of the Product Owner, a Scrum Master, and Nexus Integration Team Members.

notes.front: Besides the Product Owner, which Scrum accountability does the Nexus Integration Team include?
notes.back: A Scrum Master.
notes.explanation: The Guide says “a Scrum Master”, one person, alongside the Product Owner and the other members.
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team consists of the Product Owner, a Scrum Master, and Nexus Integration Team Members.

notes.front: Apart from the Product Owner and a Scrum Master, who else is on the Nexus Integration Team?
notes.back: Nexus Integration Team Members.
notes.explanation: These members complete the team that is accountable for a done Integrated Increment each Sprint.
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team consists of the Product Owner, a Scrum Master, and Nexus Integration Team Members.

notes.front: At scale, what dual purpose does Cross-Team Refinement serve?
notes.back: It helps teams forecast which team will deliver which PBIs, and it identifies dependencies across those teams.
notes.explanation: An adequately refined Product Backlog minimizes new dependencies emerging during Nexus Sprint Planning.
notes.evidence: It helps the Scrum Teams forecast which team will deliver which Product Backlog items. • It identifies dependencies across those teams.

notes.front: Is Cross-Team Refinement a single event, and is its format fixed?
notes.back: No. It is ongoing, and its frequency, duration and attendance vary.
notes.explanation: They vary to optimize its two purposes: forecasting which team delivers which items, and identifying dependencies.
notes.evidence: Cross-Team Refinement is ongoing. The frequency, duration, and attendance of Cross-Team Refinement varies to optimize these two purposes.

notes.front: Where is the Integrated Increment inspected, and must stakeholders wait until then to receive it?
notes.back: At the Nexus Sprint Review; but it may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint.
notes.explanation: Inspection has a fixed place, while delivery can happen earlier; either way it must meet the Definition of Done.
notes.evidence: The Integrated Increment is inspected at the Nexus Sprint Review, but may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint. The Integrated Increment must meet the Definition of Done.

notes.front: In a Nexus, who is responsible for the Definition of Done applied to the Integrated Increment?
notes.back: The Nexus Integration Team; all Scrum Teams in the Nexus must define and adhere to it.
notes.explanation: This mirrors the Scrum Guide’s rule that teams on one product share one Definition of Done.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is responsible for a Definition of Done that can be applied to the Integrated Increment developed each Sprint. All Scrum Teams within the Nexus must define and adhere to this Definition of Done.

notes.front: Who orders Product Backlog items, and who sizes them?
notes.back: The Product Owner orders them; the Developers who will do the work size them.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner can still influence sizing by helping the Developers understand and select trade-offs.
notes.evidence: The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing. The Product Owner may influence the Developers by helping them understand and select trade-offs.

notes.front: How does the Product Goal differ from the Sprint Goal?
notes.back: The Product Goal is the Scrum Team’s long-term objective; the Sprint Goal is the single objective for one Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Product Goal is the Product Backlog’s commitment, while the Sprint Goal is the Sprint Backlog’s commitment.
notes.evidence: The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team.

notes.front: A gym-booking app’s team has two statements: (1) “Become the booking app most small gyms in the region use”; (2) “Let members cancel a class from the app”. Which is the likelier Product Goal?
notes.back: A) Statement 1, the long-term objective; statement 2 fits a single Sprint’s objective.
notes.explanation: A Product Goal describes a future state of the product to plan against; a Sprint Goal is the objective for one Sprint.
notes.choices:
A) Statement 1, the long-term objective; statement 2 fits a single Sprint’s objective
B) Statement 2, because it is concrete
C) Both, pursued at once
notes.choicesExplained: B: being concrete and small suits a Sprint Goal, not a long-term objective. C: a Scrum Team works toward one Product Goal at a time.
notes.evidence: The Product Goal describes a future state of the product which can serve as a target for the Scrum Team to plan against.
